name: Adam
evidence: Genesis presents humanity as bearing the divine image and Adam as a responsible moral agent.
connection: The dignity-first reading offers a theological premise for protected rights (§1.1.5): persons have worth before an office grants them anything.
qualification: No political platform or recorded position on government liability can be attributed to Adam. This is an interpretation of a creation narrative.

name: Eve
evidence: Genesis includes female humanity in the divine-image account and names Eve as the mother of the living.
connection: A shared-dignity interpretation supports extending the bill’s protections to women on equal terms (§1.1.5).
qualification: The text records no legislative program by Eve. This entry is symbolic, not evidence that she endorsed a political institution.

name: Enoch
evidence: Moses 7 portrays Enoch’s Zion as a community without poverty and depicts his grief over human suffering.
connection: This supplies an ethical argument for measuring government by people’s welfare, relevant to poverty-based enforcement (§17.9C) and humane custody (§2.8.4).
qualification: This particular portrayal is from Latter-day Saint scripture. It is not an independently verified ancient legislative record or common to every Enoch tradition.

name: Abraham
evidence: Abraham challenges the proposed destruction of righteous people together with the wicked.
connection: The objection supports individualized responsibility and protection of innocence (§§3.2, 3.4), including when officials themselves are accused.
qualification: A plea in a theological narrative does not establish a modern evidentiary formula or endorsement of the bill’s penalties.

name: Moses
evidence: The Mosaic legal texts forbid false reports, partial judgment, bribery, oppression of strangers, and killing the innocent.
connection: These prohibitions give a religious argument for impartial adjudication and honest evidence (§§2.6–2.7; §17.4).
qualification: The Torah also contains status distinctions and punishments unlike modern equal-rights law. Select principles, not its entire legal order, are the parallel.

name: Jethro
evidence: Jethro advises Moses to select capable, truthful judges who reject dishonest gain and to distribute the work of judgment.
connection: Competence and independence from corrupt incentives fit judicial duties and training (§§2.7, 2.13).
qualification: Delegated judges under Moses are not citizen prosecution councils, and this is a scriptural account rather than a modern administrative study.

name: Shiphrah
evidence: Exodus identifies Shiphrah as one of the midwives who refused Pharaoh’s order to kill male infants.
connection: Her narrated refusal supports the principle that a superior’s command cannot excuse an obviously wrongful act (§3.7).
qualification: The story concerns refusal to kill; it does not support disregarding lawful duties or establish a general enforcement mechanism.

name: Puah
evidence: Exodus separately names Puah among the midwives who would not carry out Pharaoh’s lethal command.
connection: Her narrated conduct likewise supports personal responsibility despite official orders (§3.7).
qualification: Puah is a distinct named person in the text, but no separate political teaching or verified biography should be invented for her.

name: Samuel
evidence: Samuel publicly invites accusations of theft, oppression, or bribery and offers restitution for any proved wrong.
connection: Public answerability and repair provide a close ethical analogue to personal accountability and citizen complaints (§5.2; §17.9A).
qualification: A leader’s public accounting is not equivalent to the bill’s criminal procedures; the narrative does not establish guilt without proof.

name: Nathan
evidence: Nathan confronts King David over taking Uriah’s wife and arranging Uriah’s death.
connection: The narrative’s force is that kingship does not make an abuse morally innocent, supporting accountability for officeholders (§5.1).
qualification: Prophetic judgment is not a model for bypassing legal defense or trial; the narrative’s punishments cannot simply be imported into modern law.

name: Elijah
evidence: Elijah confronts Ahab after Naboth is falsely accused, killed, and deprived of his vineyard.
connection: The episode links manipulated legal process and wrongful property seizure, relevant to fabricated charges and property abuse (§17.2B; §17.9F).
qualification: This is a prophetic narrative about monarchy, not documentary support for the bill’s precise civil or criminal rules.

name: Amos
evidence: Amos condemns bribes, the trampling of poor people, and denial of justice at the city gate.
connection: His critique supports scrutiny of corrupt adjudication and poverty-based coercion (§§17.9C, 17.9E).
qualification: Prophetic denunciation supplies a moral standard, not evidence that every disputed government action is criminal.

name: Micah
evidence: Micah condemns leaders who despise justice and judges who act for payment.
connection: The passage supports treating public judgment as a duty rather than a commodity (§2.7; §17.6).
qualification: Religious condemnation does not supply modern offense elements or authorize conviction on rhetoric alone.

name: Isaiah
evidence: Isaiah condemns unjust decrees and administrative rules that deprive the poor, widows, and orphans of justice.
connection: This is a direct moral challenge to abuse accomplished through official paperwork (§17.9H) rather than open violence.
qualification: The book has a complex compositional history; the inference concerns the received prophetic text, not a verified modern policy position.

name: Jesus of Nazareth
evidence: In Mark, Jesus contrasts rulers who dominate others with leadership expressed through service.
connection: The servant model supports the bill’s premise that office creates duties toward people (§5.3), rather than personal entitlement.
qualification: Christian teaching also requires mercy and restraint. This passage cannot substantiate automatic approval of severe penalties or any particular prosecution structure.

name: Paul of Tarsus
evidence: Acts depicts Paul objecting to public punishment without trial and invoking legal protections against examination by scourging.
connection: The episodes support procedural protection against state coercion (§2) and the right to question an official’s legal basis.
qualification: Acts is a narrative source; Roman citizenship protections were unequal and much narrower than universal modern rights.

name: King Benjamin
evidence: Benjamin describes personal service to his people and rejects the notion that kingship makes him inherently better than them.
connection: The parallel is public service without personal superiority (§§5.2–5.3).
qualification: This is a Latter-day Saint scriptural model of kingship, not independently established history or evidence for particular offense classifications.

name: Mosiah II
evidence: Mosiah 29 proposes judges, accountability for judges who misjudge, and judgment according to the people’s voice.
connection: This is a closer textual analogue to citizen participation and review of officials (§9) than a generic appeal to righteous kings.
qualification: The chapter also warns that a people’s majority can choose wrongly. Its judicial design is not identical to the bill’s councils.

name: Alma the Younger
evidence: Alma gives up the judgment seat to devote himself to teaching after describing pride, inequality, and persecution.
connection: The account connects legitimate leadership with concern for people harmed by unequal power (§1.1.5).
qualification: Relinquishing an office and preaching are not proof of support for expanding criminal penalties or citizen prosecutorial authority.

name: Captain Moroni
evidence: Alma depicts Moroni rallying people around religion, peace, freedom, and family through the title of liberty.
connection: The stated objects resemble the bill’s protected interests (§1.1.5) and opposition to domination.
qualification: The same chapter includes coercive wartime punishment. It cannot be used as an uncomplicated endorsement of peaceful modern due process or compulsory loyalty.

name: Hammurabi
evidence: Provision 5 of the collection associated with Hammurabi imposes consequences on a judge who improperly changes a judgment, including removal from office.
connection: The narrow parallel is that judicial office need not exclude personal consequences for adjudicative misconduct (§§2.7, 5.1).
qualification: The translation and legal interpretation require care. The collection uses unequal status-based penalties and brutal punishments; it is not a charter of universal due process.

name: Cyrus the Great
evidence: The Cyrus Cylinder presents a royal policy of restoring cults and returning displaced communities and their divine images.
connection: A restrained analogy supports protection against arbitrary displacement and religious coercion (§1.1.5).
qualification: The British Museum expressly rejects calling the cylinder a modern human-rights charter. It is a royal legitimating inscription, not evidence for citizen control of kings.

sources.title: British Museum, Cyrus Cylinder collection record

name: Alexander the Great
evidence: Arrian reports Alexander punishing commanders accused of abusing subject populations, and reports that Heracon was initially acquitted before another accusation led to punishment.
connection: The limited point is official accountability for mistreating people under one’s power (§§5.2, 17.10).
qualification: Arrian wrote centuries later. Alexander’s conquest, autocracy, and executions are substantial counterweights; these episodes do not establish support for constitutional government or the bill as a whole.

name: Solon
evidence: The Athenian Constitution credits Solon with ending loans secured on the debtor’s person, allowing redress for injured others, and providing appeal to popular courts.
connection: These are concrete antecedents for accessible remedies, checks on officials, and opposition to poverty-based captivity (§2.10; §17.9C).
qualification: The account is later than Solon, and Athenian participation excluded much of the population. Popular courts were not the proposed Citizen Councils.

sources.title: Aristotle or his school, Athenian Constitution 9

name: Socrates
evidence: In Plato’s Apology, Socrates says he refused the Thirty’s command to help seize Leon of Salamis for execution.
connection: This is a strong ethical example for personal refusal of an unjust official order (§3.7).
qualification: The source is Plato’s literary account of Socrates’ defense. Refusing a wrongful order does not imply rejection of every lawful command or support for the bill’s machinery.

name: Plato
evidence: Laws IV describes the preservation of a state through the subordination of rulers to law.
connection: That provides an argument against government by an officeholder’s unchecked will (§2.1).
qualification: Other Platonic proposals are hierarchical and coercive. This principle cannot honestly turn Plato into a modern liberal democrat or defender of all the bill’s liberties.

name: Aristotle
evidence: Politics III argues for law’s authority and describes rulers as its guardians and servants.
connection: This supports the distinction between lawful office and personal domination (§§2.1, 5.3).
qualification: Aristotle also defended hierarchy and natural slavery. His restricted citizen body is incompatible with a claim that he already endorsed universal equal rights.

name: Pericles
evidence: The funeral speech presented by Thucydides praises equal justice in private disputes and public service based on merit rather than class privilege.
connection: The stated ideals support impartial adjudication and competent service (§§2.7, 2.13).
qualification: Thucydides is the intermediary. Athenian slavery, exclusion, and empire limit any inference from the speech to universal rights or modern accountability.

sources.title: Thucydides, History II.37, University of Minnesota translation

name: Cicero
evidence: On Duties distinguishes justice from injury and treats public administration as a trust directed to the advantage of those governed.
connection: The fiduciary conception supplies a direct ethical argument for officials’ duties to citizens (§5.3; §17.18).
qualification: The source’s public-duty principle is narrower than endorsing every action of Cicero’s career or every proposed criminal classification.

name: Seneca
evidence: On Clemency urges a ruler with power to punish to practice moderation rather than cruelty.
connection: This is useful for restraining coercive officials and for demanding proportional treatment of accused officials themselves (§§2, 3).
qualification: The work counsels an emperor, not citizen government. Its argument for restraint could oppose the draft’s extensive severe and capital classifications.

name: Epictetus
evidence: Discourses I.13 rebukes a master’s contempt for a servant by invoking their shared divine kinship.
connection: The equal moral standing of persons challenges the idea that rank licenses degrading treatment (§1.1.5; §5.3).
qualification: Stoic moral kinship is not a legal program abolishing status distinctions, and the passage supplies no modern enforcement procedure.

name: Marcus Aurelius
evidence: Meditations I.14 praises equal law, freedom of speech, and government that respects the governed.
connection: Those professed ideals support equal treatment and protection of criticism (§1.1.5; §17.9G).
qualification: An emperor’s private moral ideals are not evidence that his empire realized them or that he supported prosecution by independent citizen councils.

name: Confucius
evidence: Analects 12.7 makes the people’s trust indispensable to government, even when other resources must be surrendered.
connection: The inference is that public authority must earn trust through faithful conduct rather than demand it solely by title (§5.3).
qualification: The Analects is a transmitted collection, and Confucian role hierarchy is not identical to equal political participation or modern criminal liability.

name: Mencius
evidence: Mencius ranks the people above the altars of state and the ruler.
connection: That ordering supports judging public power by the welfare and rights of people (§1.1.5; §5.3).
qualification: This is a theory of legitimate rulership, not direct advocacy of the proposed councils, procedural rules, or penalty schedule.

name: Mozi
evidence: The Mohist criticism of offensive war asks why conduct condemned as individual injury becomes celebrated when rulers inflict it on a large scale.
connection: This is a sharp analogue to applying moral standards consistently across private and official conduct (§5.5).
qualification: The Mozi is a composite school text; Mohist discipline and political organization differ from modern individual-rights institutions.

sources.title: Mozi, Condemnation of Offensive War I

name: Laozi
evidence: The Dao De Jing warns that intrusive governing and proliferating prohibitions can worsen the conditions they purport to cure.
connection: This supplies a caution against regulatory domination and state-created hardship (§17.23; §17.9C).
qualification: The author’s identity and dating are uncertain. The same skepticism would challenge an expansive new criminal code, so the affinity is explicitly limited.

name: Ashoka
evidence: Ashoka’s edicts instruct judicial officers to prevent unjust imprisonment and harsh treatment, and provide a stay before execution.
connection: This is unusually concrete support for enforceable duties of humane custody and careful adjudication (§§2.7–2.8).
qualification: The inscriptions express royal policy, not proof of uniform practice. They retain monarchy and capital punishment rather than the bill’s citizen-enforcement model.

sources.title: Separate Rock Edict I; Pillar Edict IV, Dhammika translation

name: Gautama Buddha
evidence: Dhammapada 129–130 grounds restraint in recognition that others fear violence and value their lives as one does oneself.
connection: That moral symmetry supports constraints on official violence (§1.1.3) and humane custody (§2.8).
qualification: These are teachings preserved in Buddhist scripture, not a detailed legislative proposal. They also require serious scrutiny of the draft’s punitive severity.
